Most of the time I just laugh at people still crying out about election results, but this is just one of those misinformation blizzards that I feel the need to rail against. One of the things that I do as part of my job is to help design infographics. I'm still learning, but seeing misleading info in bad infographics makes me want to educate.

This is the infographic I'm talking about:

Seems harmless at first, right? Except there are a couple of things wrong. I first became suspicious when it boldly proclaimed "each figure represents 250,000 votes'. That's a random metric to measure by, so I checked a few results. First was Montana: according to Wikipedia, Trump got 274k, Clinton got 174k. But there's still a blue stick figure, so did they round Clinton's figure up by 76k (to 250k)?

So then I chose another state: New Mexico. Two blue figures, one red. According to Wikipedia, Clinton got 385k, Trump got 319k. Wait, so they're rounding up for Clinton, but down for Trump? Well, perhaps that's the only way to represent the general problem: after all, both got more than 250k. Except, look at the same situation in Maine. Clinton got 357k, Trump got 335k Hmm...a little suspect. Also, that throwaway line about "Location in each state is approximate"? Bullshit: in NM, Trump was most popular in West and Southeast districts. But that line is included for the next point.

So, fishy statistics, what else is new? Well, how about the East Coast? The figures obscure the state border lines. Is this just poor planning by the creator? Yeah, probably, but it has another effect: you can't tell which East Coast state or region a figure represents. Instead, you're forced to consider the entire mass of figures there as a whole. And guess what? Most of the figures there are blue. And the 'location approximate' line? Well, that's for isolation of red figures. Clusters of red figures never happen unless there's other greens or blues clustered nearby. This subconsciously promotes the image of isolated red voters (even when it could be as many as 350k people) or heavily contested areas.

But lastly is the concept of desaturation. This is adjusting brightness in specific colors to promote a certain type of message. The infographic uses a desaturated color scheme (which is meant to invoke playfulness) for a very specific reason. At first, it's hard to tell: after all, even a desaturated red looks different than a desaturated blue. But the reason for this is because of the third color: green. This represents 3rd party candidates, but it's almost impossible to tell at first glance where they are. Because desaturated green looks super close to desaturated blue. So at first glance, it looks like there's more Clinton voters than there actually are. In addition, desaturated red stands out much less than saturated red: so in clusters of figures, it's not as distinct (but that's a minor point).

So, what does the average user see when they view this? A few things:

  1. It's okay to dismiss essentially the Midwest. There's only 1-2 red figures there (because of the arbitrary 250k pop = 1 figure thing)
  2. There are huge clusters of blue (because of desaturated colors hiding green) in 'strongholds' like the east coast, California,etc. So more 'blue' = more population voted for Clinton.
  3. The places with the most red also had blues there (i.e contested). So it was probably super close (even when, like in Montana, it's a difference of 100k votes).
